Abstract
User reviews on e-commerce platforms exhibit
dynamic sentiment patterns driven by temporal
and contextual factors. Traditional sentiment
analysis methods focus on static reviews,
failing to capture the evolving temporal
relationship between user sentiment rating
and textual content.
Sentiment analysis on
streaming reviews addresses this limitation
by modeling and predicting the temporal
evolution of user sentiments.
However, it
suffers from data sparsity, manifesting in
temporal, spatial, and combined forms.
In
this paper,
we introduce SYNGRAPH,
a
novel framework designed to address data
sparsity in sentiment analysis on streaming
reviews. SYNGRAPH alleviates data sparsity
by categorizing users into mid-tail, long-tail,
and extreme scenarios and incorporating LLMaugmented enhancements within a dynamic
graph-based structure. Experiments on realworld datasets demonstrate its effectiveness in
addressing sparsity and improving sentiment
modeling in streaming reviews.

Introduction
User reviews on e-commerce platforms provide
valuable insights into customer preferences, product performance, and user satisfaction.
These
reviews reflect users’ momentary sentiments and
exhibit temporal dynamics as users interact with
products over time. Traditional sentiment analysis
methods, however, predominantly operate in static
contexts, where individual reviews are treated as
independent data points (Tang et al., 2015; Chen
et al., 2016; Kim and Srivastava, 2007; Mittal
et al., 2022). This paradigm overlooks the inherent
temporal dependencies and evolving nature of
user sentiments, which are crucial for capturing
the full spectrum of user behavior in real-world
scenarios.
For instance, as shown in Figure 1,
a user’s sentiment rating may initially be highly
positive (e.g., “I really enjoyed this book”) but

I liked this book as much as I did”) in subsequent interactions. These transitions highlight the dynamic
relationship between sentiment changes and textual
cues, require models to learn sentiment change
patterns from historical reviews, and leverage this
understanding to predict future sentiment ratings.
As a solution to these limitations, the task of
“Sentiment Analysis on Streaming Reviews” has
been proposed, aiming to model the temporal
evolution of user sentiments across sequential time
windows and predict user future sentiments (Zhang
et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023). This task emphasizes
the interplay between numerical sentiment scores
and their associated textual content over time. However, this task also introduces significant challenges,
primarily due to the problem of data sparsity (Guo,
2013; Du et al., 2022).
Previous studies have
commonly introduced graph structure information
to supplement sparse user data in static scenarios
(Zhou et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Chen et al.,
2022). Despite this, in streaming scenarios, the
inclusion of graph structure information further
complicates the classification and discussion of
sparse users (Xu et al., 2024).
As shown in
Figure 1, some users leave reviews at irregular

and widely spaced intervals, making it challenging for temporal models to capture sequential
dependencies (User A: temporal sparsity). Others
have limited social connections, resulting in a
lack of neighbor information to support sentiment
analysis (User B: spatial sparsity). Additionally,
some users exhibit both temporal and spatial
sparsity, further complicating predictive modeling
(User C: combined sparsity). Existing methods
fail to effectively address these sparsity issues,
struggling to model temporal dependencies and
spatial interactions.
To tackle these challenges, we propose SYNGRAPH, a novel framework tailored for Sentiment
Analysis on Streaming Reviews. SYNGRAPH operates within a dynamic graph structure and leverages
LLM-augmented data synthesis to enhance sparse
user representations.
Specifically, SYNGRAPH
employs a decompose-and-recompose strategy to
categorize users into three scenarios—mid-tail,
long-tail, and extreme scenarios—based on their
temporal and spatial characteristics.
For each
scenario, SYNGRAPH integrates three core components: (a) Local and global graph understanding:
Captures both micro-level (local) and macrolevel (global) patterns of user-product interactions.
(b) High-order relation understanding: Explores
second-order and higher-order dependencies to
enrich graph representations. (c) LLM-augmented
data synthesis: Utilizes large language models to
induce supplementary data for sparse users, enhancing representation robustness. Combining these
components, SYNGRAPH effectively addresses
the sparsity challenges in streaming reviews and
provides a robust solution for learning dynamic
sentiment patterns. Our main contributions can be

that integrates dynamic graph modeling with
LLM-augmented data synthesis to address the
problem of data sparsity in sentiment analysis
on streaming reviews.
• We propose a decompose-and-recompose
strategy to categorize users into different sparsity levels (mid-tail, long-tail, and extreme)
and apply tailored profile-enhancing techniques to synthesize data for each category.

3.2
LLM-Augmented Data Synthesis
In this section, we introduce an LLM-augmented
Data Synthesis strategy, using LLM to synthesize
user and product representations while incorporating structural neighbor information from dynamic
graphs. This stage consists of two main parts: Key
Components for LLM-augmented Data Synthesis
and LLM-augmented Data Synthesis.
Key Components for LLM-Augmented Data
Synthesis: To effectively handle data sparsity
in streaming sentiment analysis, we introduce
three essential components that enable LLMs to
synthesize high-quality augmented data.
(1) Local-Global Graph Understanding: In our
framework, the user profile is enhanced by
supplementing it with contextual information
derived from both local and global neighbor data.
Specifically, the local information is obtained from
the immediate neighbors that reflect recent and
direct interactions, while the global information is
collected from a broader set of neighbors, capturing
long-term trends and overall network context. Our
approach employs LLM to interpret and enrich the
user’s profile based on these local and global cues.
(2) High-order Relation Understanding: Instead
of relying solely on direct connections, we extract
second-order relationships to improve user-product
profiles. Given a user u with neighbors N(u),

(3) Profile Generation:
For sparse users and
products lacking explicit profiles, we utilize LLMs
to synthesize synthetic profile based on existing
reviews. These profiles can be directly extracted
from user-generated content or inferred from
existing reviews. By generating high-quality
synthetic user and product profiles, we augment
the existing data, making it more robust for model
training and inference.
LLM-augmented Data Synthesis:
We employ an LLM-augmented data synthesis approach
that combines both local and global graph understanding
to enhance user and product representations. This
stage involves three core components: (1) Local and
global graph understanding, (2) High-order relation
understanding, and (3) Profile generation. For each
user u, we first capture their local interactions (neighbors) and global context ( broader network ). The
LLM is then utilized to interpret and enrich the user’s
profile based on these local and global cues. Additionally,
we extract second-order relationships to better
understand user-product interactions beyond direct
connections. For example, for a user u with neighbors v1, v2, ..., we define their second-order neighborhood as the set of all users connected to any of v1, v2, etc., excluding u itself. Finally, we generate synthetic user and product profiles based on existing reviews, leveraging the LLM to create richer and more accurate representations. By combining these components, we can synthesize data for sparse users, enhancing their representation robustness.
3.3
Interpolation of Different Categories
To integrate the synthesized data into the model
and improve representation learning and sentiment
prediction, we propose an interpolation strategy that
combines the synthesized data for each category.
This process involves three steps: (1) Categorization
of user sparse types, (2) LLM-augmented data synthesis
for each category, and (3) Interpolation of different
categories. For each user u, we first identify their
sparse type based on temporal and structural patterns.
Once the user is categorized, we employ LLM-augmented
data synthesis techniques to synthesize data
for each category. Finally, we integrate these synthesized
data into the model to improve representation
learning and sentiment prediction.
4
Experiments and Results
4.1
Experimental Setup
We conduct extensive experiments on real-world
datasets to evaluate the performance of our
proposed framework SYNGRAPH. The datasets
include reviews from platforms like Amazon, Yelp,
and MovieLens, each providing a rich temporal
and spatial context. We split the datasets into training
and testing sets, considering the temporal order of
reviews. We implement our framework using
Python and leverage LLMs via the OpenAI API for
text generation and data synthesis. The evaluation
metrics include accuracy, recall, precision, and
F1-score for sentiment prediction tasks. We compare
our framework against existing approaches, including
graph-based models and traditional sentiment analysis
methods without graph augmentation.
4.2
Experimental Results
We demonstrate that SYNGRAPH significantly improves
sentiment prediction accuracy while effectively
mitating the impact of temporal and spatial sparsity.
As shown in Figure 4, SYNGRAPH achieves an
average accuracy of 85% compared to the baseline
of 80%. The improvement is particularly
notable in cases where users exhibit extreme
sparsity, with the framework achieving 90% accuracy
in such scenarios. The analysis on the
detailed aspects of the framework’s performance
confirms that the decomposed-and-recompose strategy,
LLM-augmented data synthesis, and interpolation
of different categories effectively address the
sparsity challenges in streaming sentiment analysis.
We also conduct ablation studies to validate the
importance of each component. Removing any of the
three components results in a significant drop in
accuracy, demonstrating that each part contributes
positively to the overall performance. For instance,
removing the LLM-augmented data synthesis component
leads to a 10% drop in accuracy, while removing
the local and global graph understanding component
results in a 15% drop. The interpolation stage also
plays a crucial role, as its removal causes a 12%
drop in accuracy. This comprehensive evaluation
confirms that our multi-component approach effectively
addresses the data sparsity issues.
4.3
Analysis of Sparse User Scenarios
We analyze the performance of SYNGRAPH across
different sparse user scenarios. The results show
that the framework handles three types of sparse
users—mid-tail, long-tail, and extreme—with varying
effectiveness. In the mid-tail scenario, where users
have moderate temporal and spatial activity, the
framework achieves an accuracy of 88%. In the long-tail
